articles.title: Tram Services Disruption in Rochdale This Weekend
articles.excerpt: No trams will operate between Freehold and Rochdale Town Centre on Saturday, with further service changes on Sunday due to maintenance works.
articles.content_html:
Transport for Greater Manchester (TfGM) has announced that there will be no tram services operating between Freehold and Rochdale Town Centre this Saturday, September 3. This disruption is part of ongoing maintenance and improvement works on the network.

Additionally, on Sunday, September 4, tram services will be affected from the start of service until 11am due to works at Deansgate-Castlefield and Trafford Bar. Passengers are advised to plan their journeys accordingly as these changes may impact travel times across the network.

TfGM has also reported that the lifts at Heaton Park tram stop are currently out of service, meaning there is no step-free access available. Customers requiring assistance are encouraged to contact the Metrolink customer service centre at 0161 244 1000 for journey planning support. The lines are open from 7am to 8pm on weekdays and from 8am to 8pm on weekends and bank holidays.

Furthermore, the lift at Derker tram stop is also out of service. Passengers travelling towards Manchester can use a ramp from Cromford Street to access the Manchester-bound platform, while those heading towards Rochdale can use a ramp and track crossing to reach their platform.

articles.title: Transport for Greater Manchester Confirms Heywood Tram Extension Project is Under Review
articles.excerpt: Transport for Greater Manchester is developing a business case for the proposed Metrolink tram extension to Heywood, which remains a potential project despite recent political changes.
articles.content_html:
Transport for Greater Manchester (TfGM) has confirmed that the proposed Metrolink tram extension to Heywood is still under consideration. This follows previous commitments made by former Greater Manchester Mayor Andy Burnham, who indicated that construction could begin by 2028. However, since Burnham's transition to Prime Minister, his successor, Bev Craig, has not mentioned the Heywood project in her recent communications, focusing instead on expanding tram services to Stockport.

The tram extension is part of the Oldham-Rochdale-Heywood-Bury Tram-Train pathfinder initiative, which aims to create a new route connecting Bury to Rochdale via Heywood. This would mark a significant milestone for Greater Manchester, introducing the first 'orbital' Metrolink route that does not pass through the city centre, as well as the first tram-train service in the region.

Despite the lack of formal approval for the project, TfGM is actively working on a business case to assess the feasibility and potential benefits of the extension. The proposed line is expected to enhance public transport connectivity, providing residents with improved access to key destinations.

As the project progresses, local residents and stakeholders will be keen to see how the business case develops and whether it will lead to formal plans for the tram extension. Further updates from TfGM are anticipated in the coming months, which will clarify the project's status and timeline.

articles.title: Middleton Library Hosts 'How to Research Your House' Event for Heritage Open Days
articles.excerpt: Middleton Library and Local Studies Centre invites residents to explore the history of their homes as part of Heritage Open Days, offering tools and skills to uncover local heritage.
articles.content_html:
Middleton Library and Local Studies Centre is inviting residents to participate in a special event titled 'How to Research Your House' as part of the Heritage Open Days initiative. This event aims to equip householders with the skills and tools necessary to delve into the history of their homes and the local area.

Participants will learn how to uncover information about former inhabitants of their properties, explore changes in the neighbourhood, and bring the history of their homes to life. The event may reveal connections to notable figures such as architect Edgar Wood and writer Samuel Bamford, as well as links to local celebrities like actress Gracie Fields and actor Don Estelle, who lived in College Bank.

The borough of Rochdale features a diverse range of homes, from modern constructions to traditional properties, including former mills and settlements dating back to the 12th century, such as St Chad’s and the area around Broadfield Park. This event provides an opportunity for residents to discover the rich history associated with their homes, which may include both celebrated and lesser-known stories.

The 'How to Research Your House' event is part of a broader effort to engage the community in local heritage. Residents interested in attending are encouraged to visit Middleton Library for more information on how to participate and uncover the fascinating history of their homes.

articles.title: Mountain Rescue Team Finds Missing 71-Year-Old Man Near Piethorne Reservoir
articles.excerpt: A 71-year-old man with dementia was located by a mountain rescue team after being reported missing near Piethorne Reservoir in Newhey. The search involved police and a helicopter.
articles.content_html:
A mountain rescue team successfully located a 71-year-old man with dementia who had been reported missing near Piethorne Reservoir in Newhey on Saturday evening. The search was initiated after Greater Manchester Police received a report of the missing individual, prompting a coordinated effort that included the use of a police helicopter.

The Oldham Mountain Rescue Team was called in to assist with the search. According to their report, the man was equipped with an air tag that indicated he was in the vicinity of the reservoir. Initial searches conducted by police, including aerial surveillance, did not yield any results, leading to the involvement of the mountain rescue team.

Upon arrival, the rescue team commenced a thorough search of the area, focusing on the water's edge and surrounding paths. Their water section utilized a raft to search the reservoir, while search dogs were also deployed to aid in locating the missing man.

The search concluded successfully when a search dog and its handler discovered the man, who was found cold and confused but alive. The swift response from the rescue team ensured his safe return, highlighting the importance of community and emergency services working together in such situations.

As Everton's U21s compete in various tournaments, including the Premier League 2 and the EFL Trophy, Edwards is likely to receive ample playing time, which could further enhance his development as a player. This transfer not only represents a personal milestone for Edwards but also reflects Rochdale's ongoing commitment to developing young footballers. The club will be looking to fill the gap left by Edwards as they aim to improve their fortunes in the league.

articles.excerpt: Norden Cricket Club maintained their position at the top of the Lancashire Cricket League JW Lees Junior Division 1, despite a defeat against Littleborough CC in a rain-affected match on 30 August 2026.
articles.content_html:
Norden Cricket Club (CC) remain at the top of the Lancashire Cricket League JW Lees Junior Division 1, despite suffering a defeat against Littleborough CC on 30 August 2026. The match, held at Littleborough, was impacted by rain, which altered the course of play significantly.

In the Rochdale derby clash, Littleborough won the toss and opted to field first. Norden were bowled out for 118 runs in 32 overs. Due to the rain, Littleborough faced a revised target of 81 runs from 25 overs, which they successfully achieved, finishing with 96 runs for the loss of 6 wickets.

In a separate match, the 1st XI game at Norden was abandoned due to the weather. Littleborough had scored 179 runs for 9 wickets in 35 overs, while Norden managed 124 runs for 4 wickets in 19 overs before the rain interrupted play.

Despite the defeat, Norden CC's position at the top of the league remains secure, and they will look to bounce back in their upcoming fixtures. The club's next match details will be announced shortly, as they aim to maintain their lead in the league.

articles.title: Why Rochdale says 'cruckle'
articles.excerpt: A short guide to a small but stubbornly local verb — what 'cruckle' means, where it comes from, and why dialect researchers care.
articles.summary: A short guide to a small but stubbornly local verb — what 'cruckle' means, where it comes from, and why dialect researchers care.
articles.body:
Anyone who grew up in parts of Rochdale will know the complaint: “I cruckled my ankle.” The word turns up in everyday speech to describe that awkward half‑twist you can walk off but which still makes you wince. That local usage — to roll or twist one’s ankle — is widely reported by speakers in and around the town and features in contemporary folk‑linguistic comments about Rochdale speech. ([eprints.gla.ac.uk](https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/330652/2/330652.pdf))

But 'cruckle' is not a modern invention. Historical dialect sources show an older verb crookle (also spelled crookle/cruckle in some records) meaning “to bend, make crooked, stoop or hobble,” and this semantic field easily covers both bending and limping actions. The English Dialect Dictionary compiled by Joseph Wright (late 19th century) records crookle in northern and midland counties with senses that match those older meanings. ([archive.org](https://archive.org/details/englishdialectdi01wrig))

How did crookle become the very local‑sounding cruckle of Rochdale? Dialectists point to two processes common in northern English: (1) onomatopoeic and imitative formation around a crook/crook‑sound family (words that suggest bending or hooking), and (2) the frequentative suffix ‑le which forms verbs that describe repeated or small actions (so crook → crookle). Older comparative work on Germanic vocabulary links this group of words to related forms in other northern European dialects, which helps explain the form and range of meanings. In short, cruckle is a predictable local survival of an older dialect verb-group. ([archive.org](https://archive.org/details/englishdialectdi01wrig))

Is cruckle unique to Rochdale? Popular memory in the borough treats it as a Rochdale speciality, and recent perceptual and crowd‑sourced mapping of Greater Manchester dialects records respondents associating the term with Rochdale specifically (you can see it listed among the keywords used when people describe the borough’s speech). That evidence shows a strong local association today, even if identical or related forms occur elsewhere historically. In other words: Rochdale speakers claim and continue to use cruckle, and that social visibility makes it feel uniquely local. ([eprints.gla.ac.uk](https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/330652/2/330652.pdf))

Where modern researchers and archivists come in: projects such as the British Library’s Word Bank and recent folk‑linguistic mapping work demonstrate how local words persist in everyday talk and are valuable evidence of small‑scale regional identity. Those projects flag items like cruckle because they show how vocabulary stays anchored to place even within a relatively small urban region. Linguists treat such items as data points for change, contact (for example, the Lancashire–Yorkshire boundary effects) and social meaning — words that signal where someone is from as much as how they walk. ([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/science/2017/nov/24/british-library-project-discovers-two-new-words-thanks-to-guardian-readers))

What should readers take away? 'Cruckle' is a neat example of how a single verb preserves sound, meaning and local pride: rooted in older dialect forms recorded by nineteenth‑century lexicographers, visible today in crowdsourced dialect maps and oral memory, and meaningful because Rochdalians still use it. It is difficult to prove absolute exclusivity — dialect words rarely obey administrative borders — but both historical dictionaries and modern perceptual research make clear why people in Rochdale continue to say 'I cruckled' rather than 'I twisted' or 'I sprained.' If you have family uses or old spellings to share, local archives and dialect projects welcome contributions — these small words are exactly the material researchers need to trace how language and place stay entwined.

articles.title: Boy, 13, stabbed in Rochdale town centre: six arrested, two bailed and stop-and-search powers extended
articles.excerpt: Live story. Six teenage boys have now been arrested after a 13-year-old was stabbed in Rochdale town centre on Saturday night. Two have been released on bail, four remain in custody, and Section 60 stop-and-search powers in the town centre run until 3pm on Tuesday. Updated as Greater Manchester Police confirm developments.
articles.content_html:
Latest, 08:30, Tuesday 1 September: six teenage boys have been arrested in connection with the stabbing of a 13-year-old boy in Rochdale town centre on Saturday night, 29 August. Two were arrested on Sunday and have since been released on bail. Four more were arrested on Monday and remain in custody. All six were held on suspicion of assault and possession of a bladed article, Greater Manchester Police said. The injured boy remains in hospital receiving treatment.

This is Rochdale Daily's single live story on the incident. It is updated in place, newest first, only when Greater Manchester Police or another primary source confirms a development. Earlier separate reports have been folded into this page; see the correction note at the foot.

What we know

The boy was stabbed during a serious assault in the town centre, near the Riverside shopping centre, on the evening of Saturday 29 August. Police described the incident as a serious assault alongside wider disorder in the town centre that night. He was taken to hospital, where he remains.

Monday 31 August: GMP confirmed four further arrests, all teenage boys, on suspicion of assault and possession of a bladed article. The two boys arrested on Sunday were released on bail while enquiries continue. Detective Superintendent Richard Hunt said the force was continuing to make progress on the investigation and that violence on the streets would not be tolerated.

Monday 31 August: the Section 60 order covering Rochdale town centre was extended until 3pm on Tuesday 1 September. Under Section 60 of the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act, officers can stop and search people in the designated area without needing reasonable suspicion.

Sunday 30 August: GMP announced two arrests and put a 24-hour Section 60 order in place for the town centre from 3pm. Chief Inspector Michael Barton, neighbourhoods lead for GMP's Rochdale district, said detectives were reviewing CCTV, gathering witness statements and analysing intelligence to identify everyone involved.

Saturday 29 August: a 13-year-old boy was stabbed in the town centre. GMP log 2750 of 29/08/2026.

What we do not know

Police have not released the boy's condition beyond confirming he remains in hospital, and have not said what led to the assault. No one has been charged. Rochdale Daily will not name anyone arrested and will not publish speculation about motive or identity while the investigation is live.

How to help the investigation

Anyone who witnessed the incident, was in Rochdale town centre on Saturday evening, or has mobile phone, CCTV or dashcam footage is asked to contact GMP on 101, quoting log 2750 of 29/08/2026, or via the LiveChat function at gmp.police.uk. Information can be given anonymously to Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111.

Story first published 30 August 2026 as "Two arrested following stabbing incident in Rochdale"; consolidated into this live page on 1 September 2026.

All those arrested are under investigation and have not been charged. Nothing in this report should be taken as an indication of guilt. It will be updated as verified information becomes available.

articles.excerpt: More than 1,300 commercial properties in Rochdale could be paying too much in business rates, with potential overpayments worth a combined £2.9 million a year, according to BusinessRateChecker.com.
articles.content_html:
More than 1,300 commercial properties in Rochdale could be paying too much in business rates, with potential overpayments worth a combined £2.9 million a year, according to research from business rates intelligence company BusinessRateChecker.com.

The company's analysis examined 8,607 commercial properties in the borough and flagged 1,308 — 15.2% — as potentially over-assessed.

That was the highest proportion of any English local authority area included in BusinessRateChecker's analysis, ahead of Maidstone at 13.8%, Kirklees at 13.7% and Mid Suffolk at 13.7%.

BusinessRateChecker estimates the affected Rochdale properties could have grounds for reductions worth around £2.9 million collectively each year, equivalent to an average potential saving of approximately £2,217 for each property it identified.

However, the findings do not allege wrongdoing by Rochdale Borough Council.

The underlying rateable value of a commercial property is determined by the Valuation Office Agency. Councils then use the relevant rateable value and multiplier when calculating business rates bills.

Rupert Spiegelberg, CEO of BusinessRateChecker.com, told Rochdale Daily that businesses also have a responsibility to ensure the property information being used is accurate.

He said: “It is actually the responsibility of the property owner to update the VOA with changes in details of floor space, floor usage etc. Different RVs are applied to different spaces in a property. Many don't.”

He said larger companies were generally more likely to scrutinise their valuations because they had the resources to employ professional surveyors, while smaller businesses could be less likely to question what they were being charged.

He added: “Large businesses are usually quite up on this and will have the resources to hire surveyors to help them but for smaller businesses like hairdressers, coffee shops etc they tend not to question the bills as much.”

How Rochdale properties were assessed

BusinessRateChecker says its system compares the rate per square metre and zoning rates of individual properties with comparable nearby premises in the same category and valuation scheme.

It then examines factors including comparable rateable values and floor areas to identify properties whose valuations appear materially different from similar premises.

The company says tolerance bands are included to avoid flagging marginal cases.

Spiegelberg also told Rochdale Daily that the 1,308 figure could be an underestimate because some properties cannot be reliably assessed by its system.

Pubs are one example because valuations can depend partly on trading information which BusinessRateChecker does not have access to.

The company's own Rochdale dataset consequently records some properties as unassessable rather than assuming they are being charged correctly.

BusinessRateChecker currently analyses around 1.9 million commercial properties across England, using the published VOA rating list alongside other data to identify properties which may warrant further investigation.

Businesses can check their own property against comparable premises through the company's online checker.

BusinessRateChecker.com — check a property: https://www.businessratechecker.com/check

Source: BusinessRateChecker.com / information supplied directly to Rochdale Daily by CEO Rupert Spiegelberg.

articles.title: REFORM UK DELIVERS: PEOPLE POWER BACKED BY REFORM SCRAPS DISASTROUS ROAD CLOSURES!
articles.excerpt: Heywood Township councillors have voted unanimously to end the Hopwood Triangle traffic trial after sustained opposition from residents, while the Coronation Avenue HGV parking restriction will remain.
articles.content_html:
Common sense has finally prevailed. At an extraordinary Heywood Township meeting last tonight, councillors voted UNANIMOUSLY to bring the Hopwood Triangle trial on Middleton Road and Magdala Street to an end and remove the road closures. The restriction preventing heavy wagons from parking on Coronation Avenue will remain in place, helping to protect local streets.

For residents, this decision has been a long time coming. The consultation results could hardly have been clearer: 86% of the approximately 700 respondents opposed the scheme. Yet despite that overwhelming response, the trial was approved and went ahead. Residents subsequently raised serious concerns about congestion, access, road safety and the effect on local businesses. People living on Manchester Road also felt they had been left out of the original consultation despite subsequently experiencing the impact of displaced traffic. The timing was another major concern. The trial began during the quieter summer holiday period, with residents warning that the true impact would become much more apparent once schools reopened and normal traffic levels returned. Last night, local people turned out in numbers to make sure their voices were heard. More than 50 residents attended the extraordinary meeting, but the size of the room at the old Police Station quickly became an issue. With residents understandably frustrated about access to a public meeting concerning their own streets, tensions rose and the meeting came close to being suspended. At that point, Reform UK Councillor Stuart Crawford intervened constructively. Recognising that many residents had already heard the Highways presentations and wanted councillors to make a decision, Stuart engaged directly with those in attendance, helped calm the situation and pressed for the meeting to move on to the vote rather than risk the evening ending without a decision. The vote was then taken. Every councillor voted to end the trial. That means the temporary road closures will now be removed, while the restriction on heavy wagons parking on Coronation Avenue will remain. And then there is the cost. The figures presented for the scheme are stark: £110,000 to install the temporary measures. That is £110,000 of public money associated with introducing and then removing a trial which had already been rejected by 86% of consultation respondents. The scheme was voted through back in November by Labour councillors Angela Brown, Paul O’Neil, Peter Hodgkinson, Peter Joinson, Susan Emmott and Liam O’Rourke, despite 86% of consultation respondents opposing it. Last night, the decision went the other way. Whatever political arguments follow, one fact should not be forgotten: local residents spoke up, kept speaking up and ultimately got the result they had been asking for. Reform UK will continue to stand with residents when decisions affecting their communities need to be challenged. A huge thank you to everybody who attended, everybody who responded to the original consultation, and everybody who refused to allow their concerns to be ignored. This was people power in action, and people power won.

articles.title: New HALO Hair & Beauty salon to open on Shawclough Road
articles.excerpt: HALO Hair & Beauty is preparing to open at 34a Shawclough Road on 1 September, with appointments already available to book and the new salon showcasing its first treatments.
articles.content_html:
A new independent hair and beauty salon is preparing to open its doors on Shawclough Road, with bookings already being taken ahead of its official launch.

HALO Hair & Beauty will open at 34a Shawclough Road, Rochdale, OL12 6LN, on 1 September.

The new salon describes itself as ‘a space to feel your best’ and has begun giving customers a first look inside the premises as it prepares to welcome its first appointments.

Images shared by HALO show a modern, neutral-toned salon interior with a dedicated reception and waiting area, alongside examples of nail treatments already being offered through the business.

Recent work displayed by the salon includes a range of manicures and nail-art designs, from understated pink finishes to French tips, floral designs and more colourful sets.

Customers are already able to book appointments ahead of the opening, with HALO directing clients to its online Fresha booking service.

The salon is also building its presence on social media under the Instagram name @_halohairandbeauty, where customers can see examples of treatments, updates from the salon and further booking information.

HALO Hair & Beauty is the latest independent beauty business to establish itself in the local area, adding another option for residents looking for hair, nail and beauty services.

Independent salons and other small businesses can play an important role in neighbourhood shopping areas, bringing services closer to residents and attracting regular local footfall.

HALO Hair & Beauty is located at 34a Shawclough Road, Rochdale, OL12 6LN and is due to open on 1 September. Bookings are being taken now through Fresha and customers can follow @_halohairandbeauty on Instagram for updates.

Have you booked an appointment at HALO Hair & Beauty, or is there another new independent business opening in your neighbourhood? Contact Rochdale Daily at news@rochdaledaily.co.uk.

articles.title: Oliver Coldman crowned champion golfer at Rochdale Golf Club Captain’s Final
articles.excerpt: Oliver Coldman has won Rochdale Golf Club’s 2026 Captain’s Final with a two-round total of 133, four shots ahead of runner-up Steve Royle.
articles.content_html:
Oliver Coldman has been crowned Rochdale Golf Club’s Champion Golfer for 2026 after winning the Captain’s Final during a weekend of competition at the club.

Coldman recorded rounds of 69 and 64 for a combined score of 133 to take the Captain’s Final title. Steve Royle finished runner-up after rounds of 67 and 70 gave him a total of 137.

The weekend also saw a series of other prizes decided. Raymond Clegg claimed Best Nett on Saturday, while Tom Wilson took Best Nett on Sunday.

Aaron Buckley won the Darren Ogden Memorial Trophy, awarded for nearest the pin in two on the 18th, with a distance of 2.13 metres. Steve George was named the lowest qualifier at 10 under par.

Rochdale Golf Club said the weekend had produced some brilliant golf despite the threat of rain, and congratulated all of the finalists and winners. The club also thanked the volunteers and staff involved in staging what it described as a special annual event.

A charity raffle was drawn during the weekend, with the club thanking supporters who bought tickets as well as the donors who supplied prizes. A full list of raffle prize winners is expected to be emailed to members over the coming days.

The Captain’s Final is one of the highlights of the club calendar, bringing together qualifiers for the concluding competition and recognising performances across the weekend.

articles.title: Inspector Approves Modern House Development Overlooking Hollingworth Lake
articles.excerpt: An appeal has granted planning permission for a new five-bedroom home at Hollingworth Heights, Littleborough, after the inspector ruled it does not harm the Green Belt.
articles.content_html:
Plans to construct a modern five-bedroom home overlooking Hollingworth Lake can proceed following a successful appeal that determined the development does not compromise the Green Belt's openness. The application, which involves replacing an existing two-storey, four-bedroom house at Hollingworth Heights on Peanock Lane, Littleborough, was initially refused by Rochdale Council.

The council's refusal was based on concerns that the proposed development represented inappropriate construction within the Green Belt, which they argued would harm its openness and negatively impact the character of the area. The existing house has a floor area of 342 square metres, while the new design would increase this to 546 square metres, representing an approximate 80% increase in volume.

Applicant Olivia McKee contested the council's decision, leading to an appeal that was reviewed by Planning Inspector Elaine Moulton. In her report, Moulton acknowledged the significant increase in volume but noted that openness is not solely determined by size. She stated that the increase in the building's footprint by 11% is modest in the context of the overall site.

The inspector's ruling allows the development to move forward, marking a significant decision for the area. The planning permission granted means that construction can begin, although specific timelines for the project have yet to be disclosed.

articles.title: Rochdale AFC installs 26 male sanitary bins to support fans after prostate cancer treatment
articles.excerpt: Rochdale AFC has installed 26 specially designed male incontinence bins at the Crown Oil Arena and joined Prostate Cancer UK and phs Group's BOG STANDARD Charter through the Back in the Game campaign.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale AFC has installed 26 specially designed sanitary bins in men's toilets at the Crown Oil Arena as part of a national drive to make live sport more accessible to men living with incontinence, including some who have undergone treatment for prostate cancer.

The club launched its involvement in the Back in the Game initiative at its home opener against Crawley Town, becoming the latest sporting organisation to sign up to the BOG STANDARD Charter run by Prostate Cancer UK and hygiene services provider phs Group.

Tobi Adebayo-Rowling helped launch the initiative ahead of the match alongside Dale director Richard Knight and Jez Williams of phs Group.

The campaign focuses on a practical problem which can prevent some men from returning to football grounds and other public venues after cancer treatment: finding a suitable place to dispose of male incontinence products discreetly and hygienically.

Rochdale AFC says specially designed bins have now been installed across its male toilets. The club has received Bronze accreditation under the BOG STANDARD Charter, which represents the installation of appropriate sanitary bins for men.

Silver accreditation also requires male incontinence products to be made available, while Gold adds a commitment to promoting awareness of prostate cancer and incontinence.

Richard Knight, who has personal experience of prostate cancer, said the club wanted supporters to feel able to return to the activities and social connections that matter to them following treatment.

He said: ‘Inclusion is important to us at the Club, and we didn’t ever want to think of any of our fans being unable to join.’

Mr Knight said seeing friends, spending time with family and attending matches can all form part of getting back into everyday life after treatment, and that the club wanted to remove a practical barrier for supporters.

WHY THE BINS MATTER

Urinary incontinence can affect men for a range of reasons and can occur following some treatments for prostate cancer. Men who use absorbent pads may need access to a sanitary bin large enough to dispose of them discreetly when away from home.

Prostate Cancer UK says prostate cancer is the most commonly diagnosed cancer in men in the UK. Its current risk information states that around one in eight men will be diagnosed with prostate cancer during their lifetime, rising to around one in four Black men.

The charity has argued that a lack of suitable disposal facilities in men's toilets can cause anxiety and embarrassment and, in some cases, discourage people from going out or returning to activities they previously enjoyed.

Nick Ridgman, Head of Support Services at Prostate Cancer UK, said the campaign is intended to make public venues more welcoming for men living with urinary incontinence and welcomed Rochdale AFC's decision to join.

The Back in the Game campaign specifically works with sports clubs because attending live sport can be an important part of people's social lives and routines. Campaign organisers said that, as of the Rochdale launch, 177 sports clubs across the UK had signed up to the BOG STANDARD, with 873 specially designed sanitary bins for men installed through the initiative.

Matthew Brabin, chief executive of phs Group, said some men can feel anxious about leaving home after prostate cancer treatment when they are uncertain whether suitable facilities will be available. He said the campaign aims to remove that barrier and help people resume normal social activities.

The wider Dispose with Dignity campaign, run by phs Group with Prostate Cancer UK since 2023, has called for better provision for men with incontinence in public toilets.

SUPPORT FOR MEN IN ROCHDALE

Anyone worried about their prostate cancer risk, going through treatment or living with its effects can contact Prostate Cancer UK's Specialist Nurses on 0800 074 8383. The charity also provides information and support through its website.

People with new or persistent urinary symptoms should seek medical advice. Urinary problems do not necessarily mean prostate cancer, but symptoms should be assessed appropriately rather than self-diagnosed.

Rochdale AFC's decision means supporters who need to dispose of male incontinence products can now do so in designated bins within the Crown Oil Arena's male toilets.

Further information about the Back in the Game campaign is available through phs Group, while prostate cancer information and support is available from Prostate Cancer UK.

Do facilities such as these make local sports venues easier to use? Rochdale Daily welcomes readers' experiences at news@rochdaledaily.co.uk.

articles.title: Are there really fairies in Healey Dell?
articles.excerpt: The rocky ‘Fairies’ Chapel’ in Healey Dell is a striking landscape feature and a long-standing folk place-name — but the historical record points to mills, viaducts and Victorian tourism, not supernatural proof.
articles.summary: The rocky ‘Fairies’ Chapel’ in Healey Dell is a striking landscape feature and a long-standing folk place-name — but the historical record points to mills, viaducts and Victorian tourism, not supernatural proof.
articles.body:
Healey Dell’s narrow gorge, tumbling river and 100‑foot viaduct make it one of the borough’s most dramatic beauty spots. Walkers are told where to find the steps down to the so‑called “Fairy Chapel,” and the Healey Dell Heritage Centre even runs a family Fairy Grotto — but how much of the Dell’s fairy lore is rooted in evidence and how much in story?

Documented history is straightforward. Rochdale Borough Council lists Healey Dell as a nature reserve rich in industrial archaeology: the River Spodden carved the gorge, powering corn, fulling and later textile mills; a disused 1800s railway and a large viaduct now form part of the trail; and the Dell is managed as a public park with a heritage centre and tearooms. (Rochdale Borough Council). A detailed local heritage survey and archaeological report prepared for the area traces ownership of Healey Hall estate, mill sites, tracks and improvements made for public access in the late 19th and early 20th centuries — including shelters and benches near the steps that lead down into the ravine below Station Road beside what is called the Fairy Chapel. (Rochdale Museums / RMNF Healey Dell Final Report, 2022). A Whitworth walking guide likewise points out the signed steps to the “Fairy Chapel” and warns that the area is uneven underfoot while noting local tales of a Fairy King and a witch.

Those are the verifiable, physical facts: a named place, carved rock niches and paths, industrial remains, and a long history of public use and interpretation. None of the archaeological or archival material in the RMNF survey treats the Fairy Chapel as evidence of supernatural events; it records landscape, ownership and industrial use, and documents the way people have made the Dell accessible and legible to visitors.

The fairy stories themselves are older, literary and folkloric. Nineteenth‑century collectors and local writers recorded tales of a “Fairies’ Chapel” and associated encounters. John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire (19th century) recounts a vivid tale in which a miller follows an enchanted hare into a crevice called the Thrutch and there beholds tiny figures issuing from a rock hollow. Victorian and later writers turned those stories into poems and popular local colour; regional folklore researchers note a fifteenth‑century–style tale surviving in local memory and printed collections. These sources show how people named and imagined particular rock niches and hollows as places where “little people” might appear, a common pattern in British and Irish topographical folklore. (Roby; local folklore surveys / Fairy Investigation Society material).

It is important to separate two things. First: the name “Fairy Chapel” and the stories attached to it are historically attested as part of the region’s folklore and nineteenth‑century literary tradition. Second: there is no primary historical or archaeological evidence that supernatural beings actually inhabited the site. Archive records and archaeological reports document mills, landowners, mapped features and 19th‑ and 20th‑century landscaping and access works — not verifiable encounters with fairies, witches or a Fairy King.

When modern visitor information talks about a Fairy Grotto or runs ghost walks and storytelling events, that is community heritage and entertainment: a way of passing on the old tales and drawing interest to a place whose atmospheric rock formations naturally invite stories. If you are curious, the best approach is to visit respectfully: the steps to the Fairy Chapel are signposted on local leaflets and the Heritage Centre can point out the precise locations where the rock hollows and carved niches encouraged the old stories.

If you are looking for proof, current authoritative sources — council pages, the RMNF heritage report and local walking guides — confirm that Healey Dell’s importance is its landscape and industrial past, and that the “fairies” belong to folklore and cultural memory rather than the archive of verifiable events. The fairies of Healey Dell endure as a local tradition that enriches the place; whether you believe in them is a matter for imagination, not the historical record.

articles.title: From teaching assistant to PT: how Rochdale mum Jen Daker found the strongest version of herself
articles.excerpt: After 16 years in education, mum-of-two Jen Daker has found a new calling as a personal trainer at The Hybrid Hut in Rochdale, combining 4am discipline, family life and a passion for helping others build confidence.
articles.content_html:
There is an obvious physical transformation in Jen Daker’s story.

She is in the best shape of her life, trains with formidable discipline and has built a new career around fitness.

But Jen’s transformation goes far beyond how she looks.

For 16 years, Jen worked at the same school as a teaching assistant. She loved education, loved working with children and, for most of her adult working life, it was all she had known.

Then she became a mum.

After two pregnancies, her priorities began to change. Fitness, which had always been part of her life, became increasingly important not simply for how she looked, but for how she felt.

“I loved working in education, but after having children my priorities changed,” she said. “Fitness helped me so much physically and mentally after two pregnancies. I realised that if I could help other people feel like that, that was what I wanted to do.”

At 36, with two young children and a mortgage, changing careers was not the easy option.

Jen did it anyway.

Today she is a personal trainer at The Hybrid Hut in Rochdale, working with women and men of different ages, abilities and levels of confidence.

At the heart of her approach is one simple principle: consistency matters more than perfection.

Jen gets up at 4am to train.

There are mornings when staying in bed would be considerably easier, particularly after a broken night with the children.

But before school runs, clients, work and everything else involved in raising a family begins, Jen deliberately creates time that belongs to her.

“My workout isn’t just about keeping fit — it’s my time,” she said. “Before the school runs, work and everything else that comes with being a mum, I get an hour that’s just for me.”

Training first thing sets the tone for the rest of her day. She feels more energetic, her mood improves and she has already done something positive for herself before everybody else begins needing her.

It is an impressive level of discipline, but Jen is quick to point out that she does not wake every morning overflowing with motivation.

“Motivation comes and goes, but habits keep you going,” she said. “Some workouts are amazing and some aren’t. Showing up is what matters.”

That is also what she wants her clients to understand.

A healthy life is not built from one heroic gym session or one perfect week.

It is built from the ordinary things repeated often enough to matter. One walk. One healthier meal. One short workout. Then another.

Jen is equally clear that she did not make such a dramatic change alone.

Behind the early mornings, late evenings and weekend sessions is a family finding ways to make it work — and she credits her partner Damien as one of the central reasons she has been able to pursue it.

“I honestly couldn’t have made such a huge career change at 36, with two young children and a mortgage, without Damien,” she said.

“There are early mornings, late evenings and weekends where we’re juggling family life around work. Having someone who believes in you, encourages you and helps share the load makes such a difference.”

Her family, she says, have supported her from day one.

That strong relationship with Damien and her obvious love for her children sit at the centre of the life she has built rather than competing with it.

Jen does not pretend the balance is effortless. Some weeks work better than others.

“I’m still figuring it out,” she said. “I’ve learnt that looking after myself isn’t selfish — it’s necessary.”

Sometimes that means a workout. Sometimes a walk. Sometimes simply finding enough time for a quiet coffee.

For Jen, exercise has increasingly become about mental wellbeing.

She describes herself as having an active mind and says she can struggle to switch off. Exercise creates headspace.

“Life can feel hectic with work and children, and training gives me time to reset,” she said.

“It’s helped build my confidence and resilience. I don’t exercise because I want to look a certain way anymore. I do it because I know how much better I feel mentally when I move my body.”

But even someone capable of getting out of bed at 4am has had to learn that discipline is not the same thing as endlessly pushing harder.

There have been days when Jen has been exhausted or overwhelmed and recognised that another intense workout was not what her body needed.

Sometimes the healthier choice is a walk. Sometimes stretching. Sometimes rest.

“Listening to your body is just as important as pushing yourself,” she said. “Fitness should support your wellbeing, not become another source of pressure.”

She admits she is still learning to follow that advice herself.

Jen’s attitude towards food is similarly grounded in real life.

She loves food. Nothing is completely off limits.

And she does not want clients spending their lives bouncing between restrictive diets and guilt.

Her philosophy is that a healthy lifestyle must still leave room for birthdays, holidays, meals out and the foods people genuinely enjoy.

“One meal or one night out doesn’t undo months of healthy habits, just like one salad doesn’t suddenly make someone healthy,” she said.

“Food shouldn’t come with guilt.”

Instead, Jen encourages moderation and habits people can realistically sustain.

“Consistency wins every time. It’s what you do most of the time that matters, not what you do occasionally.

“Celebrate birthdays, enjoy holidays and make memories. Then just get back to your normal routine afterwards.”

There is no waiting for Monday. No declaring the month ruined because of one bad day.

“It’s never too late to start again,” Jen said. “Make your next choice a positive one and keep moving forward.”

Some of Jen’s proudest results cannot be measured with scales or photographed in a mirror.

One of her earliest clients found her after seeing a recommendation on Facebook. The pair had never met.

The woman had never even been inside a gym and arrived nervous and lacking confidence.

Over time, that changed. She began trusting herself. She became comfortable training. Eventually, while Jen was away on holiday, she went to the gym on her own — something she once would never have imagined doing.

“She is like a totally different person to the woman I met,” Jen said.

For Jen, that is the real reward.

“I’ve met people who were scared to walk into a gym become confident enough to train on their own,” she said.

“Most of the time the biggest transformation isn’t physical — it’s the confidence they gain in every part of their lives.”

She sees that particularly among mothers.

Motherhood can be all-consuming. Somewhere among school runs, work, washing, appointments and everybody else’s needs, women can begin feeling that the person they once were has disappeared.

Jen understands that. And she loves watching them find themselves again.

There is another misconception Jen would happily dismantle: that personal trainers are endlessly confident.

She believes the reality can be almost the opposite.

Working every day in an environment where bodies and physical performance are constantly visible can make trainers highly critical of themselves if they allow it.

And they certainly are not expecting new clients to arrive already fit.

“Most trainers just want to help people improve, whatever their starting point is,” she said.

Jen even experienced nerves herself after recently returning from a two-week holiday.

“I got the pre-gym nerves going back,” she said.

Her message to somebody frightened of walking into a gym for the first time is straightforward. Almost everybody has felt like that. Most other people are concentrating on their own workout, not watching yours.

“Every confident person in the gym was a beginner once,” Jen said. “The hardest part is walking through the door.”

There is perhaps no such thing as perfectly balancing motherhood, relationships, work, health, friendships and everything else expected of women.

Some days one thing will inevitably win.

But Jen Daker’s story suggests women can get remarkably close.

Today, Jen offers one-to-one personal training, small-group sessions and tailored online fitness plans, working with people of all ages and abilities.

She describes The Hybrid Hut as a gym where beginners, experienced athletes, younger people and older clients are all equally welcome.

Train with Jen Daker at The Hybrid Hut.

The Hybrid Hut, Unit 1A, Moss Mill Street / Woodbine Street East Industrial Estate, Rochdale, OL16 5LB. Telephone: 07547 619709. Jen can also be contacted through her Instagram and Facebook pages, or by visiting The Hybrid Hut in Rochdale.
